title: After the Flash, One Side Would Not Move — Keraunoparalysis (Charcot's Transient Lightning Paralysis) Without External Burns — Intense Catecholamine Vasospasm vs. Stroke & Safe-Shelter Physics

teenKit.tldr: When lightning strikes, it can instantly paralyze one side of the body without leaving a single burn or scratch. This phenomenon, called keraunoparalysis, tricks our brains because we naturally assume severe danger requires visible physical damage.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It proves that nature's most dangerous forces can be completely invisible, forcing doctors and everyday people to realize that looking fine does not mean a person is safe.
keyTakeaways: Keraunoparalysis causes temporary paralysis—usually affecting the lower limbs or one side of the body—immediately following a lightning strike.
Unlike common movie tropes or high-voltage burns, a lightning survivor can experience massive internal trauma with zero external burn marks.
The temporary paralysis is typically caused by severe, shock-induced blood vessel spasms (vasopressors and catecholamines) rather than permanent nerve destruction.

vocab.meaning: A temporary, stroke-like paralysis that happens immediately after being struck by lightning.
A powerful stress hormone like adrenaline that floods the body during extreme trauma and causes blood vessels to clamp shut.
A sudden, intense narrowing of blood vessels that temporarily cuts off normal blood flow to vital tissues and limbs.
A situation or condition that seems contradictory or impossible, such as being severely injured with no visible marks to prove it.

quiz.question: What is the primary reason keraunoparalysis fools bystanders and medical professionals?
options: It only happens to people who are already sleeping.
It mimics a stroke without leaving any external burns or physical scars.
It causes the patient's skin to change to a bright neon color.
It completely erases the victim's memory of the storm.
quiz.explanation: Because there are no visible burns or broken bones, people wrongly assume the victim is completely uninjured.

quiz.question: What physiological mechanism is primarily responsible for the sudden paralysis during keraunoparalysis?
options: Intense stress hormone surges causing severe blood vessel spasms (vasospasm)
Permanent melting of the spinal cord by high-heat thermal energy
A complete and permanent shutdown of the brain's motor cortex
Total dehydration caused by the heat of the lightning flash
quiz.explanation: A massive flood of catecholamines causes blood vessels to clamp down tightly, temporarily starving the limbs of blood and movement.

quiz.question: Why does the human brain struggle to immediately process an injury like keraunoparalysis?
options: Humans are biologically programmed to only feel pain in their hands and feet.
We rely on visible cause-and-effect, like a shattered object or a bloody wound, to register danger.
Electricity is completely invisible to human eyes under all circumstances.
Medical science has only known about lightning for the last ten years.
quiz.explanation: We are deeply conditioned to look for visible physical reality, like a broken bone or laceration, to validate that trauma has occurred.
